event.title: Korea Week | Korean Food: Culture, Politics, and Identities: Rory Walsh, University of Michigan
event.description:
Korean food is having a moment–one that's been decades in the making. Dr. Rory Walsh explores what Korean food is, how it got that way, and how it's changing under our noses. From Ann Arbor to Seoul, this talk explores what food has to do with tradition, identity, international politics, ancient history, family, self, and, of course, the deceptively complicated concept of authenticity.

Rory Walsh has been studying the anthropology of Korea since 2012, and has eaten her way across the peninsula (and Jeju!). She has written extensively on Korean archaeology and hosts the UM Nam Center for Korean Studies' podcast, "Korea in Maize and Blue: How Did You Get Here?", interviewing Korean scholars and other professionals across disciplines.

This event is part of Korea Week, and is held in partnership with the Ann Arbor District Library and the Korean Cultural Center of Washington D.C. For more information, visit https://myumi.ch/9JJ4g.

*If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.*

event.title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
event.description:
Curated by Srimoyee Mitra

Stamps Gallery kicks off the fall 2026 semester with an ambitious mid-career survey of interdisciplinary artist Cosmo Whyte. Born and raised in Jamaica, Whyte completed a BFA from Bennington College and earned an MFA from the University of Michigan. He is currently a faculty member at the School of the Arts and Architecture, UCLA.

This exhibition brings together two central concerns that animate Whyte’s artistic practice: the archive, both personal and public, as a site of disturbance; and migration as a lived experience of refuge, refusal, and reinvention. In Whyte’s work, the archive is never static or neutral. Rather, it is a contested space where official histories encounter memory, inheritance, and the fragments of stories carried across generations. His practice moves within this charged interstitial terrain, between what has been recorded and what has been remembered, between institutional knowledge and embodied experience. Whyte invites the viewer to consider the fluidity of geographic borders and layered cultural identities that have persisted despite societal unrest caused by racial and socio-economic hierarchies across generations. In an era of intensified border politics and renewed debates over national identity, Whyte’s work offers a timely meditation on memory, movement, and belonging.

Presented with support from the U-M Institute for Humanities, the U-M LSA Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, and the U-M Library.

event.title: Algebraic Geometry Seminar: Crepant resolutions via stacks: Jeremy Usatine, Florida State University
event.description: Consider an invariant that behaves nicely for smooth varieties, such as Euler number, Betti numbers, or Hodge numbers. Suppose we want a version of this invariant for singular varieties that sees interesting information about the singularities. I will discuss how this naturally leads to the notion of crepant resolutions of singularities. However, crepant resolutions (by varieties) are rare in practice. I will discuss joint work with M. Satriano in which we show that crepant resolutions actually exist in broad generality, as long as one is willing to consider algebraic stacks. Specifically, any variety with log-terminal singularities admits a crepant resolution by a smooth algebraic stack. As one consequence, in joint work with J. Huang and M. Satriano, we obtain a cohomological interpretation for Batyrev's stringy Hodge numbers. This talk will not assume familiarity with stacks.

Join award-winning forager, outdoor educator and James Beard Award winner Alexis Nikole Nelson for a lively conversation about wild foods, sustainability and the rich cultural traditions connected to the plants growing all around us. With more than five million followers across Instagram and TikTok, Nelson has become a beloved social media creator known for her joyful and informative foraging videos. She inspires audiences to see the natural world in a new way while exploring the intersections of food, history and environmental stewardship. Through storytelling, humor and practical insights, she invites us to reconnect with the land—and maybe discover a few tasty surprises hiding in plain sight. 

Nelson will be signing her new book, "Happy Snacking, Don't Die!" Booksweet will have them available for purchase while supplies last. Purchase in advance from Booksweet. 

This event will be moderated by Will Brinkerhoff, a SEAS agroecologist, chef and science communicator.

event.title: Community Story Exchange: Facilitated by Narrative 4
event.description:
*"You tell my story, I tell yours. In the first-person. Face to face." *
    * –Colum McCann, co-founder of Narrative 4*

Held in conjunction with The Stories We Carry, featuring acclaimed novelist Colum McCann in conversation with Michigan Public's April Baer (https://myumi.ch/NXrg9), this facilitated workshop offers the opportunity to put the evening's ideas into practice. Participants will pair with another attendee, share a personal story in response to a common prompt, and then retell their partner's story in the first person—a powerful exercise in empathy, perspective-taking, and human connection.

No storytelling experience is required. Whether or not you attended the preceding conversation with Colum McCann, you are welcome to participate. Space is limited, and advance registration is suggested. Register to attend the story exchange at https://forms.gle/pQP3PbMdD3LvZ3tQA.

Narrative 4 is a global nonprofit that believes stories can change the world. Co-founded by acclaimed novelist Colum McCann, Narrative 4 brings people together through its signature Story Exchange, an evidence-informed practice that invites participants to share a personal story and then tell their partner's story in the first person. Used in schools, universities, and communities around the world, the Story Exchange cultivates empathy, deep listening, and meaningful human connection across lines of difference.

event.title: Astronomy Colloquium | AI Discovery in Physics and Astronomy: Dr. Cecilia Garraffo
event.description:
AI may change how science answers its hardest open questions, and even which questions it asks. Today's vast datasets hold physical information we do not yet know how to look for, and AI offers a way to search for the unexpected. To trust AI discoveries, we need to judge models by whether they obey the laws of physics. How convincing their outputs look is not enough. In this talk I will discuss the promise and challenges of cutting-
edge AI for science, and how to define and build physical realism into our models. I will present recent progress
on physical, probabilistic, and generative models for astronomy. I will also show where classical physics
models, machine learning, and agentic AI each reach their limits.
